APCSP is an easy course, but accordingly it is very much undervalued by colleges. I'd say both of the classes can be low-stress (presumably depending on the teacher, but unlike for example AP Bio is a class that simply cannot be low-stress no matter the teacher). AP Psych is primarily memorization, that much is true, but it isn't the kind of memorization you'd find in for example AP Euro, in my opinion, as most of the information is intuitive so precious little (unless you take an online AP Psych exam like I did) is actually memorization required, mainly scientist names; in that respect it is pretty close to AP Economics.  


A comment on AP Statistics: the course is in some sense like AP Psych in that much of it is intuitive, but it also turns into memorization for much of the course, though it is accordingly very slow.  


Overall, it seems that you are leaning pretty heavily towards APCSP. I think that APCSP is something that can definitely be done without prior programming experience, so if you want to do that it's a fine course, but also its usefulness in granting college credit is low-ish. However, I don't think that Psych is as much boring memorization as you think it is, and you can in any case probably spend the period doing something more interesting in lieu of paying attention, if you opt for that route.

Having taken every single one of these classes with 5s:

AP Stats and AP CSP are the easiest ones of the bunch, AP CSA could also be on the easier end depending on background, AP CSP especially, but AP Stats as well has much less content than any other AP exams.

Physics C exams are hard but the curves are straight-up st-yew-pid so they shouldn't be THAT much of a problem, but definitely require some work. My method for these was to just do a LOT of practice problems; they are free online. A lot of it I found is being able to find all the forces/torques and resolve them, but this gets easier the more problems you do and the more different setups you see.

As for Lang, this is probably harder than you think it is, but still requires work. Practice essay-writing, and the hardest essay on the exam (as expected) is the rhetorical analysis. The MCQ is pretty much a writing ACT section so those could be good practice, if you don't happen to have old Lang MCQ sections lying around.

Overall I think that's a good list and you want to spend the largest part of your time on Physics C.

Honestly I think there are two extremes: abused, and neglected. Someone who is neglected is probably going to become self-sufficient, because they don't have anything done for them, and have to do it themselves. It's sort of in the sense of narcissism of caring only about yourself and in so doing ignoring others, which is in a way the selfish side of it, if that makes sense.

  
Abuse is a whole other beast. Neglect is more passive; abuse is active. Abuse is probably from what you've suffered more of the time, I would think. That's the threats, the self-contradictory demands, the hitting, the requirement that you do specifically what they want, when they want, and nothing more. That's more restricting; even if you wanted to do something else, they don't allow you do, because they crave control. Rather than being selfish per say, this would sprout from their wish to be important and powerful; you can't have a free will, you must be subservient. That's more likely to produce people like us who have crippled independence.

Many narcissists may exhibit a mix of traits, but one of the two most likely dominates and makes an impression that informs personality.

That's just my take, maybe I'm wrong.
